🇺🇸 The SEC has just made it easier to securitize certain US data centers and I think it is a pretty major development as the question is no longer just how far AI can progress technologically, but who will end up carrying the risk.

➡️ The SEC now considers that certain data-center securitizations do not necessarily need to comply with all the requirements imposed on traditional ABS, including some post-2008 rules such as risk retention. The logic is that a data center is a physical asset that remains in place and continues generating revenue after the debt has matured and this matters mainly because it makes capital recycling easier.

💰 A developer can build a data center, secure contracts with Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta or CoreWeave, stabilize the revenues and then refinance or securitize the infrastructure. That debt can subsequently be bought by insurers, pension funds or fixed-income investors, while the developer gets some of its capital back and can start building the next facility. If every company had to keep every data center permanently on its balance sheet, the cycle would eventually run into financing constraints. Securitization dramatically expands the pool of investors capable of funding the buildout.

🫧 The structure of the current cycle is beginning to show some similarities with the Dotcom Bubble. A technological revolution can be completely real and still generate massive overinvestment if the financial system becomes capable of financing infrastructure faster than final demand grows.

⚠️ This is very bullish for the duration of the AI cycle in the short and medium term, but potentially much more concerning for credit markets over the longer run. Who is going to pay for all this CAPEX? The answer is increasingly becoming the entire financial system. The real warning signal will come when projects can continue getting financed regardless of their underlying economics simply because Wall Street always knows where to redistribute the debt.

At that point, AI will no longer be just a technological revolution, it will have become a gigantic credit-creation machine.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/R0cHQUtTrN

*IMF chart: https://t.co/nV7SHGZ8gk

How much of a crowded trade’s demand would remain if momentum stopped?

Funded crowding has support from cash flow, organic spot demand or supply sinks that can persist after momentum fades. Borrowed crowding depends more heavily on leverage and momentum moving through a thin float.

Once the market turns, the recovery depends on whether those sources of demand are still in place.

There's a sticker in every restaurant window saying somebody inspected the place.

Nobody checks when.

It gives the same energy as getting a smart contract audit only once.

Azimuth found 4 confirmed critical vulnerabilities in the past month alone. All four were in code that had already been audited.

Four in a month isn't a huge sample, but all four sitting in audited code is the part that got my attention.

The report was accurate the day it shipped, then the contracts changed, new integrations got bolted on, and the path that actually mattered was never in scope for the original review.

AI can generate security reports all day. The hard part is figuring out which findings are real, and that's what @testmachine_ai is doing with Azimuth.

Instead of flagging something as "possibly exploitable," it recreates the attack and checks whether it actually works.

The interesting part is that every validated finding also gives Azimuth better data to improve future investigations.

More useful testing creates better security signals, which makes the system stronger over time.

That's also where their new Points system fits in. Contributing useful, validated findings can unlock more Azimuth access, features, rewards, and recognition over time.

I don't think this replaces audits. Audits still catch things a running system won't. But treating one review as permanent coverage stopped making sense a while ago.

Pleased to partner with TestMachine AI on this one.

tweets.text:
One of the most honest reads on enterprise AI returns⬇️

Jane Street just raised $14.6B in senior secured notes, the largest bond deal ever by a non-bank market maker. The 10-year tranche priced at 8.088%. Primarily a refi of a $5.5B floater and an $11B debt load, but tech infrastructure and trading expansion are stated uses.

What makes this rare: Jane Street is one of the largest disclosed non-tech internal-GPU users, and one of the few with publicly priced debt against it: 4,032 liquid-cooled GPUs in Dallas, ~$6B committed to CoreWeave plus $1B of equity, early work on a self-financed 100-200MW build, targeting 10x into the hundreds of thousands.

They sell no compute and no inference. The chips forecast asset prices. The output is directly monetized and the funding cost is observable.

So, the bar is computable: At CRWV's 6-year depreciation life and 10% salvage, $100 of Jane Street capex must throw off $20.33 (20.3%) annually for six years plus $10 back at the end to set NPV at zero against 8%, 10-year money.

Salvage assumptions barely move it. Every 10 points of recovery buys only ~136bp annually: 25% salvage requires an 18.3% cash yield, etc.

So Jane Street is carrying 8% money against a ~20% break-even, even on modest salvage assumptions. Nobody with their track record takes that trade casually, a real signal about what monetized AI output can earn when someone can actually measure it.

It's also a signal about what the bond market will underwrite: $14.6B, ten years out against a "six-year asset," no NVIDIA residual backstop, clearing on conservative salvage assumptions. Which leaves room for these rates to come down if and as the fundamentals materialize and for IG borrowers to try the same trade on even better terms.

I see $STAA earnings today as net positive. To be honest, I thought the stock should be up 10% rather than down 4% after this report but once again, you never know what’s priced in.

Revenue was $93.5M, China grew another 10% sequentially to $52.3M, the company made $8.1M and generated $19.7M in operating cash flow. They now have around $181M in cash and investments and no debt.

More importantly, these earnings remove a lot of the fear around China. The business is clearly alive and China seems to be stabilizing.

Margins are still the weak point, but some of the pressure looks temporary. ERP costs are elevated and tariffs are still hurting gross margins. The most important thing for me is the new Swiss factory. China is by far STAA’s largest market, and by year-end the plan is to manufacture 100% of China-bound lenses in Switzerland, which should remove the U.S.-China tariff problem.

This also changes the picture if Broadwood ever decides to push for a sale again. When the previous $30.75 offer was made, there was full-blown fear that the China business was basically dead. With China stabilizing and the business profitable again, it should be much easier to create a competitive sale process. STAA is a very niche business with technology and distribution that could have significant strategic value and synergies for several potential buyers.

In my opinion, this report removes much of the extreme downside scenario because it shows the underlying business is valid and recovering.

I’ll wait for the earnings call later today to get the full picture.

First Principles Ep. 7 with Noam Nisan

More than 30 years ago, Gödel Prize winner @noamnisan helped develop a proof technique he never expected anyone to use in the real world.

Today, the sum-check protocol sits at the heart of some of the fastest modern SNARKs. Nisan traces its unlikely journey from early work on interactive proofs and IP = PSPACE to practical systems for verifiable computation.

But Nisan’s career also tells a broader story about how research responds to technological change. When the web arrived in the 1990s, he deliberately left a field in which he was already a leading researcher to understand a new problem: How do you get independent actors on the internet to cooperate when they have different incentives?

That question helped give rise to algorithmic game theory — and, decades later, brought Nisan back to questions around blockchain fees, token economics, and protocol design.

Hosted by @Tim_Roughgarden with @SuccinctJT

At what point do we admit that all AI agent products are kinda similar: connect your email, calendar, docs, Slack, cloud, whatever. The agent will then extracts a ton of context about how you work, who you work with, how you communicate, what you care about to turn that into markdown memory files & then an orchestrator on top that learns your patterns and tries to reproduce them.

The frontier isn’t really “chat” anymore. It’s proactive background agents. Users don’t prompt the AI. Agent notices something needs to happen and does the work on the behalf of the user. 

And underneath, a lot of it is surprisingly simple conceptually: give the model more context, give it tools, memory, and some cron jobs / triggers / routines.

So the actual game is becoming: who can build the best memory, take the most useful actions, and do it while burning the fewest tokens. Because it’s actually pretty easy to build an amazing personal memory system if you’re willing to spend $100+ per user. The hard part is getting 95% of that quality for $5. The goal is the highest quality context and actions, lowest inference cost to get the highest gross margin.
